records.name: Jalisco
records.current_summary:
No Jalisco-specific statutes, votes, lethality figures or incident records are supported by the vetted sources for this map. The national picture governs: by March 2025 an international human-rights organization counted 22 of Mexico's 32 states as having legislated legal gender-recognition procedures, with six state legislatures enacting none; a March 2024 report documents that where no procedure exists, trans people face police stops, denied documents and institutional mistreatment.

Transfeminicide has become a criminal category in some states — the capital imposes up to 70 years — against more than 95% homicide impunity nationally, and reporting finds convictions lag the statutes. For a visitor, Jalisco's own documented record is thin on this map: expect the country-wide picture rather than verified local protections or verified local hostility.

sources.claim: National framework (HRW, 31 Mar 2025): legal gender recognition in Mexico is set state-by-state — as of March 2025, 22 of the 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, two more run one in practice without enactment, six legislatures have enacted none, and only seven states extend recognition to children. Mexico's Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to minors in 2022; the Inter-American Court likewise requires a simple, accessible procedure. HRW documents the consequences where no procedure exists (identity-document mismatch driving discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco). For this record: the national mosaic, not any locally enacted certainty, is the operative framework.

HRW/Community Center for Inclusion report (6 Mar 2024) on a Mexican state lacking a legal gender-recognition procedure, documented in Tabasco: without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries violence, harassment and humiliation risk, excluding trans people from employment, health services, education and financial transactions; context includes the Aug 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa and more than 95% of homicides nationally going unpunished in 2022. For this record it is the operative evidence of what 'state law silent' means for trans people on the ground.

records.name: Nayarit
records.current_summary:
Nayarit was the first of Mexico's 32 states to criminalise transfeminicide, introducing sentences of up to 60 years in early 2024 — a step the capital followed in July 2024 with its 70-year 'Paola Buenrostro law', named for a trans sex worker murdered in 2016 whose attacker was released after 48 hours despite footage and witnesses and has not been caught since. Nayarit's law also lets friends, not only relatives, claim bodies and drive investigations, which matters where families disown trans relatives.

That statute landed against more than 95% impunity for homicides in Mexico in 2022, believed higher for transfeminicides, so it records official posture more than proven protection. No other Nayarit-specific incidents or enforcement records are supported by the vetted sources; the national picture otherwise governs — by March 2025 an international human-rights organization counted 22 of 32 states as having legislated legal gender-recognition procedures, with six enacting none.

sources.claim: Nayarit-specific entry: a 2017 reform of the state Civil Code established an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, allowing adults to change identity documents to match gender identity. The 31 Mar 2025 national roundup counts 22 of Mexico's 32 states as having legislated such procedures, EIGHT with none and two more practice-not-law (the record's 'six states' wording should read eight). The document also records the 2019 national Supreme Court guidelines and that only seven states extend recognition to children.

Names Nayarit as the FIRST of Mexico's 32 states to criminalise transfemicide, introducing sentences of up to 60 years earlier in 2024; Mexico City followed in July 2024 as the second, with up to 70 years (Paola Buenrostro law). The law also lets friends - not just relatives - identify and claim bodies and drive investigations, relevant where families disown trans relatives. Context: in 2022 more than 95% of homicides in Mexico went unpunished, the figure believed higher for transfemicides.

records.name: Queretaro de Arteaga
records.current_summary: A split record: Querétaro's congress banned conversion practices on 29 June 2023 with penalties of 2-6 years, yet it is one of six states Human Rights Watch (March 2025) lists as having never legislated any legal-gender-recognition procedure, leaving trans people's identity documents permanently mismatched. No state-specific incident or enforcement evidence was identified.
records.current_localsOnly: The absence of a recognition procedure is a resident-documentation issue; its visitor relevance is the climate signal of the refusal.

sources.title: Gender Recognition in Mexico by State | Human Rights Watch
sources.claim: Human Rights Watch's state-by-state table states, under Querétaro, that the state has not reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure for transgender people (as of the March 2025 map, which counts 22 of Mexico's 32 states as having legislated). This is the jurisdiction-specific basis for the record's statement that Querétaro is one of six states HRW lists as never having legislated any legal-gender-recognition procedure.

sources.title: Terapias de conversión: Pese a ley aprobada, hay más pendientes legislativos para comunidad LGBT+ - Tribuna de Querétaro
sources.claim: Tribuna de Querétaro reports (20 September 2023, with Frente Queretano por el Derecho a la No Discriminación spokesman Walter López) that the reform to Querétaro's Penal Code prohibiting Esfuerzos para Corregir la Orientación Sexual y la Identidad de Género (ECOSIG), commonly called 'conversion therapies', was published and is in force; it sets a penalty of two to six years in prison, a fine of 20 to 2,000 times the UMA and 50 to 100 hours of community service, treating such practices as discriminatory and torturous under articles 1 and 6 of the Inter-American Convention to Prevent and Punish Torture; the group calls it a milestone compared with states where the ban remains unpublished but says a first generation of LGBTIQ+ reforms is still pending. This corroborates the record's claim that Querétaro's congress banned conversion practices with 2-6 year penalties, sourced to a Querétaro outlet.

records.name: San Luis Potosi
records.current_summary: No region-specific incident, enforcement or ordinance evidence was found; the state's place in the national map is ordinary compliance: a 2019 reform of the Civil Registry Law created an administrative legal-gender-recognition procedure, with implementing regulations set by gubernatorial decree.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Mexico (Wikipedia)
sources.claim: Wikipedia's Mexico-wide LGBT rights article carries San Luis Potosí-specific facts: on 17 May 2019 the state began authorizing legal gender changes for transgender people, and on 21 May 2019 same-sex marriage took effect after the state Congress voted 14-12 in favour on 16 May 2019, with joint adoption by same-sex couples legal in the state from the same month. The article lists San Luis Potosí among the states that enacted a gender-identity law in 2019 and among those whose hate-crime statutes recognize motivation by gender and sexual preference, while noting its local law bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender but not gender identity. This confirms the record's claim of a 2019 civil-registry reform creating an administrative gender-recognition procedure and adds the marriage and adoption dates a trans visitor would rely on.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Mexico (Wikipedia)
sources.claim: Wikipedia's Mexico-wide LGBT rights article reports Sinaloa-specific events: the Mexican Supreme Court ordered the state to legalize same-sex marriage within 90 days on 15 May 2018, and the Sinaloa Congress passed a same-sex marriage law on 15 June 2021, with civil unions for both same-sex and opposite-sex couples performed in the state. The same article lists Sinaloa among states whose local law bans discrimination on grounds of both sexual orientation and gender identity, among those with hate-crime statutes covering gender and sexual preference, and among the states that enacted a gender-identity recognition law, dated 2022 there. That 2022 dating conflicts with the March 2025 HRW count cited in the record's existing sources that Sinaloa had legislated no legal gender-recognition procedure, so the state's actual local-law status needs verification against the state code before relying on either account.

sources.claim: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time; the underlying source is a Human Rights Watch country overview (31 March 2025) on transgender rights progress and challenges in Mexico, headlining that 22 of the country's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure by that date and naming six whose legislatures had enacted none.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Mexico - Wikipedia (state-by-state coverage including Sonora)
sources.claim: The page's state-by-state coverage names Sonora as one of the 25 Mexican states that have legislated a gender identity law, with Sonora dated to 2020, giving trans people a statutory procedure to rectify gender on civil documents. It further records that Sonora's Congress banned conversion therapies (ECOSIG) on 6 December 2022, and that Sonora is among the states whose hate-crime laws recognize motivation by gender and sexual preference and which ratified the 2011 constitutional amendment prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. On marriage, the page records that by 31 December 2022 every Mexican state, including Sonora, had legalized same-sex marriage by legislation, executive order or judicial ruling. For this record: concrete Sonora-specific legal protections (gender-recognition procedure, conversion-therapy ban, hate-crime framework, marriage availability) that the current summary said were unsupported by vetted sources.

sources.title: Aprueban Ley de Identidad de Género en Sonora - El Sol de Hermosillo
sources.claim: Hermosillo-based daily El Sol de Hermosillo (article dated 1 October 2020) reports that Sonora's Congress approved the state's Gender Identity Law ("Ley de Identidad de Género"), under which people who identify with the opposite gender can modify their official documentation. For this record: local-news confirmation that Sonora legislated a gender-recognition procedure for trans people in 2020, the state-level fact the country dossier currently lacks, and one of the procedures counted in the report that 22 of Mexico's 32 states have enacted such laws.

records.name: Tabasco
records.current_summary:
Tabasco has enacted no legal procedure for recognising gender identity. A Human Rights Watch report co-produced with a local inclusion centre (March 2024) documented that the absence of any recognition procedure leaves trans people's identity documents permanently mismatched and exposed to police and institutional mistreatment.

By March 2025, Human Rights Watch counted 22 of Mexico's 32 states as having legislated legal gender recognition and named six — among them Tabasco, the subject of the dedicated 2024 report — whose legislatures had enacted none. For a visible trans visitor the document mismatch is the practical trigger: an ID that does not match presentation invites the questioning and mistreatment the report records.
records.current_localsOnly: The recognition vacuum binds residents hardest in daily institutional life — identity papers, services and detention treatment — per the HRW 2024 report's documentation.

sources.claim: Tabasco-specific entry: the state has NOT reformed its legislation and has no legal gender recognition procedure - one of EIGHT states with none (record said 'six'; two more states are practice-only). Documented consequence: where no procedure exists, mismatched identity documents invite police stops and institutional mistreatment.

Tabasco-dedicated HRW report (6 Mar 2024, produced with a local community centre for inclusion): Tabasco has no legal gender recognition procedure, so trans people's identity documents never match their gender, curtailing rights across four socio-economic areas. Example: Karina Gómez, a trans woman, murdered in Tabasco in August 2023. For this record: direct on-the-ground documentation of the documentary mismatch that endangers visible trans people in Tabasco itself.

records.name: Tamaulipas
records.current_summary:
Tamaulipas is among the six Mexican states whose legislatures have enacted no legal procedure for recognising gender identity, per Human Rights Watch's March 2025 count of 22 of 32 states having legislated one. Where no procedure exists, trans residents' identity documents remain permanently mismatched with any official record of who they are.

The consequences of that absence are documented in the companion 2024 Human Rights Watch report on one such state: mismatched documents invite exactly the police checks and institutional mistreatment that most endanger a visible trans visitor in daily interactions.
records.current_outOfScope: Blanket armed-group violence along the border affects every traveller regardless of gender expression; the trans-specific element is the documented targeting and extortion of trans women by those same actors, which the assessment covers.

sources.title: Gender Recognition in Mexico by State | Human Rights Watch
sources.claim: HRW's state-by-state table (31 Mar 2025) records that Tamaulipas 'has not reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure for transgender people', placing it among the eight Mexican states with no procedure at all, against 22 of 32 states that have legislated an administrative procedure (two more have one in practice only). For a trans person whose documents are issued in Tamaulipas this means there is no administrative route to change identity documents to match their gender identity, which is the record's core claim.

sources.title: Aprueban en Tamaulipas sanciones contra terapias de conversión y ataques a la identidad de género - NT | Noticias de Tampico Tamaulipas
sources.claim: On 18 June 2025 the Tamaulipas state Congress unanimously approved reforms to the local Penal Code adding a chapter on crimes against sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression, explicitly banning 'conversion therapies' with prison terms of 2-6 years and fines of up to 2,000 UMA; penalties rise by half when victims are minors, disabled or elderly, or in subordinate settings such as family, medical or workplace. Dated evidence that Tamaulipas's criminal law protects gender identity even though the state still lacks an administrative gender-recognition procedure.

sources.title: Comunidad LGBT+ y diputadas acuerdan agenda conjunta por identidad de género y salud en Tamaulipas - NT | Noticias de Tampico Tamaulipas
sources.claim: On 4 February 2026 deputies of Tamaulipas's 66th legislature and LGBT+ civil-society groups (including Tamaulipas Diversidad, Vihda Trans A.C., Tendremos Alas A.C. and La Resistencia Trans) agreed a joint agenda to push a Gender Identity Law and anti-discrimination and health reforms, noting the initiatives have been pending since June 2025 and that the absent law keeps limiting trans people's access to health, education and employment. Confirms that as of early 2026 no legal gender-recognition procedure exists in Tamaulipas and a Gender Identity Law remains unpassed.
